displayQuote: Hope is the dream of a waking man

meta.title: Who really said "Hope is the dream of a waking man"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Aristotle — via his ancient biographer Diogenes Laërtius (Lives V.18). The wording is C. D. Yonge’s 1853 translation of the reply on hope.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Hope is the dream of a waking man'?
meta.ogDescription: Yes, Aristotle — but recorded by Diogenes Laërtius, not written by Aristotle himself. ‘The dream of a waking man’ is C. D. Yonge’s 1853 rendering.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 384–322 BC · Greek philosopher; founder of the Lyceum
answer.sourceLine: The line is a genuine Aristotle saying — but a reported one. It survives in Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers V.18, a list of Aristotle’s witty replies: asked what hope is, he answered “the dream of a waking man.” That exact wording is C. D. Yonge’s 1853 translation ↗; R. D. Hicks’s Loeb renders the same reply “a waking dream.” It is not found in any of Aristotle’s own surviving treatises — the biographer recorded it roughly five centuries after his death.

source.excerpt: Once he was asked what grew old most speedily, and he replied, ‘Gratitude.’ On another occasion the question was put to him, what hope is? and his answer was, ‘The dream of a waking man.’
trail: Wikiquote lists the line in its sourced Aristotle section — not Disputed or Misattributed — citing Diogenes Laërtius, trans. C. D. Yonge, p. 187 ↗.
The primary source is Diogenes Laërtius, Lives V.18; the Perseus/Hicks text ↗ gives the same reply as “a waking dream.”

The precise popular wording — “the dream of a waking man” — is verbatim from C. D. Yonge’s 1853 translation ↗: “the question was put to him, what hope is? and his answer was, ‘The dream of a waking man.’”
source.excerptNote: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives V.18, trans. C. D. Yonge (1853). The hope reply sits amid a run of Aristotle’s apophthegms.

author.name: Aristotle
author.heading: About Aristotle
author.metaLine: 384–322 BC · Greek philosopher & polymath; founder of the Lyceum
author.bio: Aristotle of Stagira (384–322 BC) studied under Plato, tutored Alexander the Great, and founded the Lyceum in Athens. His surviving treatises — on logic, ethics, physics, biology, poetics and politics — shaped Western thought for two millennia. This particular saying, however, comes not from those works but from a collection of his reported bons mots preserved by the later biographer Diogenes Laërtius.

misattribution.heading: What’s muddled about it
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Aristotle is genuine, but two things get widely confused — the exact wording, and where the line actually comes from.

items.why: This shorter form (used by BrainyQuote, Forbes and others) and “the dream of a waking man” are not competing quotes — they are two translations of the identical reply in Diogenes Laërtius: R. D. Hicks’s Loeb gives “a waking dream,” while C. D. Yonge’s 1853 text ↗ gives “the dream of a waking man.”

The line appears in none of Aristotle’s surviving treatises. It is an apophthegm recorded by his biographer Diogenes Laërtius, Lives V.18 ↗, roughly five centuries after Aristotle’s death — a reported saying, not a written one.

misattribution.truthLine: The attribution holds: Aristotle, asked what hope is, answered “the dream of a waking man” — as preserved in Diogenes Laërtius, Lives V.18 (C. D. Yonge, 1853 ↗).

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: Diogenes Laërtius devoted a passage of his life of Aristotle to the philosopher’s quick, aphoristic replies. Asked in turn what a friend is, what grows old fastest, and what hope is, Aristotle answered each with a single memorable image. Hope, he said, is what a waking person dreams — a vision entertained with the eyes open.

The metaphor has outlived its source. Detached from Diogenes Laërtius and Aristotle’s surrounding wit, it now circulates as a standalone motto of optimism, its two-translation split (“waking dream” vs. “dream of a waking man”) rarely noticed by those who share it.
detailsBody: In Yonge’s rendering the hope reply is immediately preceded by “Once he was asked what grew old most speedily, and he replied, ‘Gratitude,’” and followed by the anecdote of Diogenes the Cynic offering Aristotle a dried fig.
context.pull: Hope is what a waking person dreams — a vision held with the eyes open.
